reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The contact quality is historic on both sides of the ball: a .411 xwOBA and .585 xSLG as a hitter, a 2.72 xERA and 30.4% whiff rate as a pitcher. The strikeout rate at the plate, 23.0%, is the one drag on an otherwise elite Statcast batting profile, and the 13.1% walk rate does a lot to offset it, but Ohtani remains someone who runs into swing-and-miss trouble despite contact that is almost always punishing when it connects. On the mound, the 98.1 mph fastball feeds a profile that keeps barrels down to 3.8%, which is why the underlying numbers look like a staff ace rather than a curiosity. The projection at 694 PA, .290/.389/.560 with 40 home runs, is what it is: the floor is still a superstar, and the ceiling is what happens when you remember he does both.

Albies sits at the 9th percentile in xwOBA and 8th in hard-hit rate, contact metrics that explain why the .251/.309/.420 projection looks about right even with 25 projected home runs attached to it. The power comes from volume and a pull-side approach, not from the quality of contact — a 4.3% barrel rate and 86.9 mph average exit velocity are bottom-fifth marks, and that's a profile that lives and dies by whether he squares up the few balls he does elevate. What saves him is the strikeout rate: 13.9% is genuinely good, which means he's in play enough for the counting stats to accumulate across 689 projected plate appearances. He's a second-division regular who earns a lineup spot through contact frequency and durability, not a hitter you're building around.

reports.name: Eury Pérez
reports.published_report: 98.3 mph fastball velocity paired with 2677 rpm spin is the kind of combination that makes a pitching profile loud before you even look at the results. Pérez's 26.9% strikeout rate and 28.6% whiff rate hold up, but a 9.9% walk rate undercuts the whole package — contact quality against him is middling at worst, so the damage comes from the base-on-balls column. If the command tightens, a 3.37 ERA over 158.9 innings with 174 strikeouts describes a mid-rotation anchor worth building around; if it doesn't, that elite spin stays decorative and the profile stalls somewhere between promising and maddening for a 23-year-old.

reports.name: Michael Busch
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the load-bearing wall here. At 12.5% BB%, Busch draws free passes at a clip that lands in the 85th percentile, and that discipline is what props a .331 xwOBA over a .234 xBA — his exit velocity (88.1 mph) and hard-hit rate (39.0%) are both below average, so the contact itself isn't the story. The projection translates that into a .348 OBP against a .244 average, which is exactly the shape you'd expect: a first baseman who reaches base more than he hits. If the zone command slips and pitchers stop respecting the bat enough to nibble, the whole profile compresses toward a second-division bat with ordinary power.

reports.name: Cristopher Sánchez
reports.published_report: A 36.9% chase rate sits in rarefied air, and paired with a 5.6% walk rate, it explains everything about why Sánchez works. Hitters swing at his stuff outside the zone constantly and make contact when they do connect, but the contact is soft enough at 89.3 mph average exit velo that it hasn't hurt him yet — where the Statcast card gets complicated is a 41.8% hard-hit rate that runs well below the median for good pitchers, suggesting his xERA of 3.34 is closer to his true talent than a 2.59 projection ERA implies. The profile hinges entirely on that chase rate holding: if hitters start laying off, the strikeout rate (27.8%) erodes and there isn't premium velocity to fall back on. If the chase stays, he's a legitimate mid-rotation horse worth every bit of 205.8 innings.

reports.name: Chandler Simpson
reports.published_report: Zero barrels. That's the profile in one number, and everything else builds from it: 83.9 mph average exit velocity, a 13.7% hard-hit rate, and an xSLG sitting at the 2nd percentile. What saves him is that he almost never swings through anything, a 10.5% whiff rate in the 99th percentile, and he puts enough bat on ball to sustain a .260 xBA even without any thump behind it. The shape of the projection is .305/.335/.365 across 599 PA, a guy who runs his way to relevance with 45 projected stolen bases and 96th-percentile sprint speed to make the 62 projected runs plausible. The whole thing hinges on keeping the strikeout rate at 8.5% and staying healthy enough to let the legs do their work, because if pitchers solve him for walks, his 4.4% BB rate at the 5th percentile means there is no power cushion waiting to bail him out.

reports.name: Logan Gilbert
reports.published_report: The contact profile is the one wrinkle in an otherwise clean picture. Gilbert's walk rate sits at 5.8%, his whiff rate at 30.1%, and hitters are chasing at 32.7% — the command-and-miss combination that makes a 3.33 ERA projection over 187.5 innings believable. What keeps the xERA at 3.68 rather than something prettier is the contact quality when he does get hit: a 41.5% hard-hit rate and 10.2% barrel rate that run well above what his strikeout profile would suggest he allows. The read is that Gilbert is a genuine mid-rotation workhorse who doesn't miss bats cheaply, and the profile holds as long as his ability to limit walks keeps the hard contact from clustering into damage.

reports.name: Payton Tolle
reports.published_report: The 36.1% chase rate is the engine here. Tolle gets hitters to expand, and the contact they do make is soft enough that his xERA sits at 2.72 while his actual ERA projects a half-run higher, the gap suggesting some strand-rate regression is already baked in. His 27.8% strikeout rate is legitimate for a starter, and the 6.7% walk rate means he's not trading control for the chases he earns. The profile hinges on that chase number holding at this level, because his 27.5% whiff rate is good without being dominant, so if hitters start laying off, the strikeouts compress and he becomes a back-of-rotation arm running on contact management rather than a near-ace running on both.

reports.name: Brandon Marsh
reports.published_report: The tension in this profile is the gap between the contact shape and the discipline that's supposed to support it. A 37.5% chase rate sitting at the 11th percentile is genuinely damaging, and a 6.1% walk rate near the bottom of the league means he's generating whatever production he gets almost entirely through contact quality. The good news is the contact quality holds up: a 45.1% hard-hit rate and an xBA of .262 suggest the bat-to-ball, when it connects, is real enough to translate into the .269 projection. He's a solid-average outfielder who produces a useful line, projected at 20 home runs and 13 steals across 589 plate appearances, so long as pitchers don't bury him in the zone and let the chase rate spiral, because if they do, the 6.1% walk rate offers no floor to fall back on.

reports.name: Sam Antonacci
reports.published_report: The contact profile here is legitimate and unusual: a 15.1% whiff rate and a 21.9% chase rate together describe a hitter who makes consistent, disciplined contact, yet his 87.5 mph average exit velocity and 34.8% hard-hit rate say the bat isn't doing much damage when it connects. That gap between plate discipline and raw impact is the whole tension in this profile — the .278 xBA makes sense, the .402 xSLG flatters him a little, and the 22 projected stolen bases (projection) tell you the value has to come from getting on base and running, not from driving the ball. If the speed ages or the 7.4% walk rate doesn't climb to support the on-base game, what's left is a slap-contact center fielder with below-average power and a questionable glove (9th-percentile OAA). Works as an everyday piece if the legs stay sharp; a second-division regular otherwise.

reports.name: Oneil Cruz
reports.published_report: The exit velocity sits at 96.1 mph with a 17.2% barrel rate, both at the absolute ceiling of the Statcast scale, and the xSLG is .500 to match. That's a genuine plus-plus power profile buried inside a player who strikes out 35.0% of the time and whiffs at 37.6%, which is why the projection lands at .806 OPS rather than something that looks like the underlying contact quality. Cruz is the rare case where the bat-to-ball problem is so severe that it legitimately suppresses what the quality-of-contact numbers promise, and everything hinges on whether he can trim the chase rate enough to let the damage show up more consistently. If the contact improves even modestly, the .500 xSLG and 28 projected steals combine into a fantasy profile that outpaces the .806 headline; if it doesn't, you're paying for power you can only partially capture.

reports.name: Shane McClanahan
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile tells a story of a pitcher still finding himself after Tommy John: a 4.18 xERA and 22.2% K rate that sit right around league average, with hard contact numbers that lean in the wrong direction. What still works is the 26.9% whiff rate and a 31.7% chase rate that suggest he can still manipulate bats, even if he's not burying the strikeouts at his old clip. The 3.37 ERA projection over 136.5 innings assumes his ERA-to-xERA gap closes, and that's the hinge — if the hard contact rates (8.7% barrel, 41.5% hard-hit) don't improve, the projection looks like a best-case outcome rather than a baseline. Right now he profiles as a mid-rotation arm rebuilding toward something better, but the Statcast numbers make the upside a hope rather than a given.

reports.name: Hunter Brown
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument. Brown's Statcast profile reads like a legitimate mid-rotation arm, with 85.9 mph average exit velocity, a 6.3% barrel rate, and stuff that generates whiffs at a 26.2% clip, but a 13.7 BB% sits at the 5th percentile and that single number bleeds into everything else. Hitters can't punish him when they do make contact, yet he keeps putting them on base for free, which is why the projection lands at a 1.29 WHIP despite the contact suppression being genuine. If the walk rate compresses toward league average, he's a reliable mid-rotation starter in Houston's system; if it stays where it is, the 109.7 projected innings and 3.69 ERA both look optimistic.

reports.name: Mickey Moniak
reports.published_report: The gap between his .413 xSLG and his .218 xBA is almost comically wide, and that's the whole profile in one tension. Moniak's 10.8% barrel rate is legitimate thump, but a 41.3% chase rate at the 4th percentile means he's handing pitchers the blueprint to neutralize it — the power only shows up when they let it. The projection (.259/.301/.510, 24 HR in 442 PA) is essentially a bet that Coors Field inflates his contact numbers enough to mask a chase problem that Statcast says is severe. If the walks stay at 5.5% and the chasing doesn't improve, what's left is a streaky corner bat with real pop and a roster question attached.

reports.name: Jacob Wilson
reports.published_report: The contact skill carries this profile and the power does not. Wilson's 11.6% strikeout rate sits in the 95th percentile, his whiff rate is 14.8%, and those two numbers explain why a guy with an 84.1 mph average exit velocity keeps finding his way on base at all. The problem is a 3.6% walk rate that offers no cushion when pitchers learn to exploit his 42.3% chase rate, and an xSLG of .345 that leaves almost no margin for the projection's .706 OPS to hold across 493 plate appearances. A .300 xwOBA sits in the bottom fifth of the league, the 36.0% chase rate explains why, and nothing in the contact quality, a 6.3% barrel rate and 36.2% hard-hit mark that both sit well below average, suggests he's beating the ball hard enough to compensate. The projection's .259/.313/.421 line across 578 PA is probably the ceiling, not a baseline, and it only gets there because 29.0 ft/s sprint speed is genuinely elite and drags the counting stats into respectability. If the zone discipline doesn't improve, this profile collapses toward a good-athlete bench piece who can't stay in a lineup long enough for the speed to matter.

reports.name: Cole Carrigg
reports.published_report: The sprint speed and stolen-base projection tell the same story: 28.8 ft/s, 15 projected steals, a guy who earns his way onto a lineup card with his legs before the bat has to do anything heavy. The .274/.349/.450 projection across 377 PA is a legitimate everyday-outfielder line, and the 9 projected home runs make clear the ceiling here is a speed-and-contact regular rather than a middle-of-the-order piece. His 79th-percentile fielding grade says he can hold a corner without embarrassing anyone. The whole profile hinges on whether the contact quality holds at the big-league level — if it does, he's a solid second-division regular with real stolen-base value; if it fades, the speed alone leaves him as a useful bench bat but probably short of a starter's role.

reports.name: Nick Gonzales
reports.published_report: The .282 xBA sitting in the 90th percentile while average exit velocity checks in at 86.3 mph — that gap is the whole profile. Gonzales makes contact at an elite rate and puts it where defenders aren't, but he doesn't hit the ball hard enough to generate much power, which is why the xSLG (.386) and barrel rate (2.7%) both sit near the bottom of the league. The projection filling out to a .300/.356/.400 line across 628 PA is believable precisely because the contact quality metrics support a high average, and his 28.8 ft/s sprint speed adds a layer of value that soft contact hitters need to survive. Everything hinges on the hit tool continuing to translate: if pitchers find a way to suppress the average, the 6.5% walk rate and eight projected home runs leave almost nothing else to carry the line.

The discipline profile is the honest constraint — 42 walks against 93 strikeouts in 455 AAA plate appearances translates to a walk rate and a strikeout rate that both land right at MLB average, which means the bat has to carry him with no margin for a power regression. reports.name: Caleb Durbin
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact profile is almost entirely about bat-to-ball skill, and the power numbers are genuinely soft. A 2.9% barrel rate and 83.9 mph average exit velocity sit at the very bottom of the league — the 15 projected home runs and .407 SLG lean heavily on volume and luck outrunning an xSLG of .329. What keeps him relevant is a 13.5% strikeout rate that barely anyone matches, paired with 21 projected steals and a fielding profile that grades well at third. If the speed and contact translate into the kind of on-base pressure the projection suggests, he's a useful everyday player; if pitchers keep the ball away from his barrel and the BABIP normalizes downward, you're left with a light-hitting, fast third baseman who doesn't walk enough (7.5%) to make up the difference.

reports.name: Cam Caminiti
reports.published_report: The 3.70 ERA across AA & A+ looks good; what's underneath it is more complicated. Caminiti's 106 strikeouts in 97.6 innings translate to a 7.8 K/9 at the MLB level, a tick below what MLB starters average, and his 45 walks push his translated BB/9 to 4.3 against an MLB mean of 3.2. The 1.20 WHIP with an 85th-percentile mark in his pitcher pool suggests he's managing contact well enough to keep the walks from fully cashing, which is the load-bearing beam in this profile right now. If the command develops and the walk rate comes down, he's a back-end starter; if it doesn't, you're left with a depth arm who lives on contact suppression longer than he should have to.

reports.name: Dillon Dingler
reports.published_report: Thirty-one projected home runs from a catcher is a number worth taking seriously, and the Statcast profile gives you a reason to. His .358 xwOBA and .488 xSLG both sit in the upper tier of the batting percentile card, and the gap between those expected marks and his actual production last season suggests the bat plays better than the results have shown. The engine isn't raw power volume, as his 88.9 mph average exit velocity sits near the middle of the league, but a 10.6% barrel rate translates contact quality into damage at a rate his exit velocity alone wouldn't predict. The real liability is plate discipline: a 33.8% chase rate near the bottom of the league caps his on-base ceiling and is the one thing that keeps .319 OBP from being the floor rather than the ceiling.

reports.name: Cam Smith

reports.name: MacKenzie Gore
reports.published_report: The contact quality numbers are the tension in this profile. An 8.8% barrel rate and 42.0% hard-hit rate, both in the bottom quarter of the league, suggest Gore is getting hit harder than his strikeout rate implies, and the xERA of 3.84 sits roughly a half-run better than the 4.28 projection precisely because the projection factors in the contact risk the Statcast surface is revealing. The 25.8 K% is genuine production, but the 8.5 BB% keeps the profile from being elite, and the whiff and chase numbers are solidly above-average without being dominant. What he actually is: a volume innings starter who misses bats at a useful rate, keeps the ball in the yard often enough, but gets tagged when contact happens, and if the walk rate climbs, the ERA follows while the gap between xERA and projection closes in the wrong direction.

reports.name: Ryan Weathers
reports.published_report: The 3.55 ERA projection feels like a kindness the Statcast profile hasn't earned yet. His xERA sits at 4.20 and the contact quality numbers, a 41.1% hard-hit rate and 89.4 mph average exit velocity, belong to a pitcher who has been hit around more than the ERA column suggests. The strikeout rate at 25.4% and walk rate at 6.9% are both above average, and the 27.0% whiff rate tells you hitters aren't just making routine contact, but the 29.2% chase rate is below average and that's the mechanism the whole profile leans on: if he can't expand the zone, the whiffs dry up and the ERA catches up to the xERA. At 169 projected innings with 12 quality starts, the ceiling here is a back-end starter who survives on command and sequencing; if the contact numbers don't improve, what's left is a long man in a good bullpen.

A 26.6% strikeout rate drags against an xBA of .255 and an xwOBA of .323 that say the underlying contact quality is roughly league-average, so the gap between what he's hitting and what he should be hitting isn't a skills problem, it's a strikeout problem. reports.name: Kyle Harrison

The one thing to watch: his chase rate of 32.5% is the softest piece of the profile, meaning the strikeout output depends more on in-zone swing-and-miss than on hitters expanding — if that whiff rate erodes, the walk rate becomes load-bearing in a hurry. reports.name: Nelson Rada
reports.published_report: The bat-to-ball profile is loud, and it's the whole argument. At AAA in 2026, Rada is hitting .281 with an 18% strikeout rate across 473 plate appearances, and the MLB translation puts his contact at a 20% K rate against a league that strikes out at 22% — a genuine edge that holds across a full-season sample. The problem is everything else: a .084 ISO at AAA translates to .092 in the majors while the typical big leaguer sits at .150, and 32 stolen bases matter a lot more when the power ceiling is that low. Either a bench bat or a platoon piece at best, and it stays there unless the game power that's missing at 20 shows up when he fills out, because without it the contact skill is just enough to keep him employed, not enough to make him an everyday player.

reports.name: Chase Meidroth
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact profile is bottom-fifth at every power metric, 87.8 mph exit velocity, 4.5% barrel rate, .334 xSLG, and yet the projection still lands at .270/.348/.400 across a full 653 PA. That gap is almost entirely explained by the plate discipline: a 19.1% whiff rate and 27.4% chase rate that both grade well above average, letting him manufacture contact and walks where a free-swinger with the same raw power would bleed out. The profile translates to a useful table-setter if the strike-zone reads hold at this level, and a light-hitting utility piece if pitchers start attacking him with more conviction and the chase rate creeps up. His 94th-percentile OAA marks him as a genuine defender at second and short, which is the floor-raising detail that keeps him a regular rather than a bench name even in the pessimistic scenario.

reports.name: Carter Jensen
reports.published_report: The contact metrics are a contradiction wrapped in a catching profile. Jensen makes enough contact to hurt you, 90.6 mph average exit velocity and a 10.0% barrel rate, but a 29.9% whiff rate drains almost all of it before it reaches the expected-average column, where his .199 xBA sits near the bottom of the league. The 25.1% chase rate is genuinely good discipline, which means the whiffs are coming inside the zone, and that's a harder fix than simply learning to lay off. If he squares up contact the way his exit velocity suggests he can, the projection's 20 home runs in 593 plate appearances is plausible for a catcher; if the in-zone swing-and-miss doesn't come down, he's a backup who hits the ball hard in short bursts and disappears in longer looks.

Either a fringy everyday regular if the contact improves, or a bench bat whose walks keep him employed.

reports.name: Jhoan Duran
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.22 and the xwOBA at .232, both at the 99th percentile, and the surface ERA of 2.01 in the projection isn't flattering the underlying numbers — the underlying numbers are earning it. His 35.0% strikeout rate pairs with a 4.5% walk rate, a combination that leaves almost no margin for hitters to work with, and a 2.9% barrel rate explains why the 40.4% hard-hit rate hasn't done much damage: contact happens, but squared-up contact almost never does. The one tension in the profile is that 100.4 mph fastball running against 2074 rpm of spin, low enough that hitters who do make contact may start timing it if they see him enough in a pennant race. The profile hinges on whether that ride holds up over a full Philadelphia season; if it does, 34 saves and a sub-2.22 ERA is a realistic outcome, and if the fastball gets predictable, the strikeout rate is what carries him.

reports.name: Bryce Elder
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is almost perfectly median, which is both the argument for him and the ceiling on it. His xERA sits at 4.03 and his xwOBA at .310, both right at the 50th percentile, which says the results aren't hiding anything ugly underneath, but they're not hiding anything exciting either. What keeps the floor from dropping is a 6.5% barrel rate that grades above average, because hitters aren't squaring him up even when they do make contact, and that's the whole mechanism: Elder gets by on weak contact rather than swing-and-miss, with a 19.5% strikeout rate and 21.6% whiff rate that both sit in the low twenties percentile-wise. The dependency is ball-in-play luck, and his 92.4 mph fastball at the 12th percentile leaves him with little margin if his contact-management slips even a grade.

reports.name: Gage Miller
reports.published_report: The .398 OBP is the headline, and the discipline behind it holds up in translation. Across AAA & AA this season, Gage Miller has walked 35 times against 43 strikeouts in 246 plate appearances, and when that contact-to-walk shape moves to an MLB context, his K% translates to 20.6 against a league that sits at 22.0, with his walk rate coming in well above average at 10.9%. The ISO translates to .155, right at league average, which is where the ceiling caps out: if the gap power doesn't grow, you're looking at a disciplined platoon bat who gets on base and doesn't embarrass you, not a regular. The floor is a bench piece, and the whole profile hinges on whether that .309 BABIP across AAA & AA reflects real contact quality or gets squeezed at the next level.

reports.name: Theo Gillen

Either a useful everyday center fielder or a very good bench bat who can run.

reports.name: Eduardo Quintero
reports.published_report: The .445 OBP and 40 stolen bases in 431 A+ plate appearances will get your attention fast, and the 75 walks make the on-base number feel earned rather than fluky. What the translation punctures is the power: his ISO at A+ is .188, but the MLB-equivalent reads .135, which is shy of where most big-league bats land, meaning the offense at higher levels is going to live and die by the hit tool and the legs. The strikeout rate translates to 24.2% at the MLB level, not a killer but enough margin for error that a dip in BABIP from the current .392 would expose him quickly. If the contact and speed hold, there's a useful player here; if the hit tool regresses once spin gets more sophisticated, you're left with a profile that runs well but doesn't impact the game enough to stick.

reports.name: Bryan Reynolds
reports.published_report: The tension in Reynolds's profile is that .347 xwOBA sitting inside a strikeout rate that keeps bleeding runs off the table. His 13.5% walk rate is elite-tier contact avoidance from pitchers, and the 46.4% hard-hit rate explains why the expected slugging matches his projected .425 SLG nearly point for point. But a 29.0% whiff rate against a chase rate of just 25.3% means pitchers are getting him inside the zone, and the .246 xBA tells you that contact, when it happens, isn't finding grass at the rate his exit velocity would suggest. If the strikeout rate holds where it is, he's a .259-type hitter with a big walk and real power, an everyday outfielder who reaches base at a .363 clip and does enough damage to earn 704 projected plate appearances.

Across AA & A, Ortiz has drawn 35 walks against only 36 strikeouts in 203 plate appearances, and that discipline translates to an 11.7% MLB-equivalent walk rate while the big leagues average 8.5% — a gap wide enough to carry an otherwise ordinary bat. The .386 OBP does real work; the .239 average doesn't, and a .255 BABIP suggests he isn't catching many breaks on contact. If the ISO, which translates to .135 at a time when MLB sits at .150, stays where it is, you're looking at a get-on-base bench bat rather than an everyday third baseman, and the ceiling between here and a platoon role hinges on whether the power takes a step forward as he faces better pitching full-time.

reports.name: Sean Sullivan
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one decent thing here. At AAA in 2026, Sean Sullivan has issued 19 walks across 54.7 innings, and that control translates to a 3.3 BB/9 MLB equivalent, essentially matching the MLB average. The problem is that everything else in the translation lands below the median: a 7.9 K/9 against an 8.6 MLB-average mark, and an 11.7% K-BB% trailing the 13.5% baseline, meaning the command advantage isn't generating enough swing-and-miss to cover for it. If the stuff plays up in shorter bursts, he could carve out a multi-inning or setup role; if it doesn't, he's organizational depth.

reports.name: Jack Mahoney
reports.published_report: The ERA is the eye-catcher, 2.50 across AAA & AA, and it's earned enough attention to note — but the strikeout translation is where the profile gets honest. Seventy-five punchouts across 81.3 innings sounds like a workhorse, but that 8.3 K/9 at the minor-league level translates to 7.5 at the MLB equivalent, short of where most major-league starters live, and the walk rate comes back slightly elevated too, leaving a K-BB% that translates to 10.9% when the majors typically run 13.5%. The ERA does real work right now; the swing-and-miss does not, and if the contact management that's suppressing hits in the minors doesn't travel, what's left is a guy who walks too many hitters he can't put away. Either a multi-inning reliever who pitches to contact and survives on sequencing, or a depth arm when the margins tighten.

reports.name: Andrew Morris
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.97 and hitters are barreling him at just 3.5%, which tells you the quality of contact he's suppressing is genuine — average exit velocity of 86.6 mph backs that up. The catch is that his 26.2% chase rate is near the bottom of the league, meaning he's getting weak contact without generating much swing-and-miss outside the zone, and that's a narrower path than the xERA makes it look. If hitters start laying off and forcing him into the zone more, the strikeout rate at 22.2% doesn't give him much margin to work with. He's a real weapon in the Minnesota bullpen when the contact-suppression holds, but this profile lives and dies on batters continuing to put bad swings on pitches they should take.

reports.name: Edgardo Henriquez
reports.published_report: The contact quality numbers are almost absurd: a 2.5% barrel rate and 25.8% hard-hit rate that together produce an 83.3 mph average exit velocity, all three sitting at the very top of the Statcast leaderboard. That's not a pitcher who misses bats occasionally — Henriquez simply does not allow good contact, and a 2.64 xERA says the underlying quality matches the results. The problem is the 11.4% walk rate, which is where the profile gets honest about its limits, because a reliever throwing 100.5 mph with a 29.6% whiff rate and a 34.0% chase rate who also walks more than one in nine batters is leaving leverage on the table every time command slips. If he ever gets that walk rate to a neutral level, the projected 3.24 ERA looks conservative for a Dodgers setup arm with this stuff; if he doesn't, 12 holds and a 1.12 WHIP is still a useful reliever, just one the manager has to watch carefully in tight spots.

reports.name: Max Meyer
reports.published_report: The spin number is the story: 2614 rpm on the fastball puts him at the 98th percentile, and that's what the 28.6% whiff rate is built on, not velocity. The 95.1 mph heater is roughly league average, so Meyer is winning with movement and deception rather than raw heat, which explains the 26.2% strikeout rate alongside an 8.9% walk rate that still needs tightening. His xERA sits at 3.87 while the ValuCast projection has him at 2.81 over 125.0 innings, and that gap comes down entirely to whether he can suppress hard contact more consistently — the 42.0% hard-hit rate and 8.6% barrel rate both suggest hitters are catching up to him more than the ERA would indicate. If the contact quality stays where the Statcast profile says it is, the ERA regresses toward the xERA; if he sharpens the walk rate and gets a little lucky sequencing, the projection holds.

reports.name: Dylan Crews
reports.published_report: The contact and walk numbers are the ceiling suppressors here. Crews runs a 30.6% whiff rate and a 6.9% walk rate, a combination that explains why the xwOBA sits at .320 despite genuinely above-average raw power, a 10.3% barrel rate and 90.6 mph average exit velocity that both grade comfortably above the midpoint. The projection (.218/.288/.368) reflects that gap between what he hits when he connects and how often he fails to. He's a 93rd-percentile runner with real fielding value, so the floor is a useful, cheap fourth outfielder, but the ceiling hinges entirely on whether he can close the whiff rate enough to let the contact quality breathe into an everyday profile.

reports.name: Orion Kerkering
reports.published_report: The contact suppression numbers are genuinely striking: a 29.1% hard-hit rate and 85.0 mph average exit velocity put him at the very top of the reliever population, and an xERA of 3.13 says the soft contact isn't random. The problem is the walk rate. An 11.9 BB% is a significant liability for a high-leverage arm, and the chase rate of 28.7% explains why — he isn't generating enough early exits to cover for the free passes. If the command tightens, the xwOBA of .275 suggests a reliever who profiles in genuine setup work, which the projection reflects with 18 holds across 63.4 innings; if it doesn't, the 3.63 ERA projection is probably optimistic, and he settles into a middle-relief role where the contact suppression is appreciated but the margin for error never fully opens up.

reports.name: Wilder Dalis
reports.published_report: The surface numbers are loud — .300/.394/.555 across A+ & A, with 16 home runs and 25 stolen bags in 332 plate appearances, but the translation is where the conversation gets honest. That .254 ISO in the low minors collapses to .153 at the MLB-equivalent level, essentially matching what a league-average hitter produces, which tells you the plus raw power at 19 is contact quality against soft competition, not a preview of middle-of-the-order damage. The 24% strikeout rate translates to 28% at the MLB-equivalent level, and that gap is the hinge: if it doesn't improve as the arms get sharper, the .300 batting average goes with it, and what's left is a bench-caliber third baseman. A 13% walk rate is encouraging enough to keep the floor from being nothing, but this profile needs the contact to hold two levels higher before you can argue for more than organizational depth.

reports.published_report: The power is loud enough to earn your attention, but the profile around it is a genuine concern. Nineteen home runs at AA with a .297 ISO at 22 years old is a real signal; the slugging translates to an .197 MLB-equivalent ISO, which clears the bar most first basemen need to justify a roster spot. The problem is that 30 K% at AA translates to a 30.2 K% equivalent against major-league pitching, and for a first baseman without other carrying tools, that's a lot of ground to cover with the bat alone. The .364 BABIP is doing some work on the batting average, so the contact picture is already softer than the .283 looks; if the strikeout rate firms up even modestly, there's a second-division regular in there, but if it doesn't, what remains is a one-dimensional slugger with a narrow path at a position that demands more.

The raw power translates to a .140 ISO at the MLB level, roughly matching what an average big-league hitter produces, but a K% that would run 35.1% in the majors means he'd be striking out at a rate that makes even the power hard to deploy. Everything hinges on whether he can make enough contact to let the pop matter, and right now, 164 strikeouts in a single AAA season says he can't.

reports.name: Fenwick Trimble
reports.published_report: The speed-power combination is louder than the ceiling. Eighteen stolen bases and 14 home runs across 350 AA plate appearances is a real offensive toolkit, and the .199 ISO confirms the pop isn't just a counting-number trick at a hitter-friendly level. The translation is where it gets honest: that ISO dials down to .151 at the MLB level, landing right at league average, and the walk rate translates to 7.9% against a league that runs at 8.5%, meaning the on-base profile doesn't carry the slugging when the power compresses. If the speed ages well and the hit tool (.263/.340 in AA) holds its shape, he's a useful fourth outfielder who runs into value; if the contact doesn't sharpen at Triple-A, you're looking at an organizational depth piece in the Marlins' system.
